items.text: KEY POINT

items.label: text
items.text: You may have noticed by now that hydrogen does not really fit into the Periodic Table properly. Although it has 1 electron in its outer shell, it is not in Group 1 because it does not have similar properties to the other elements in Group 1: it is not a metal and does not have similar chemical properties to the alkali metals.

items.label: text
items.text: If a basic oxide is soluble in water it will dissolve to form an alkali. For example, sodium oxide reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide solution, an alkali. If an acidic oxide is soluble in water it will dissolve to form an acidic solution. For example, sulfur(IV) oxide reacts with water to form sulfurous acid.

items.text: DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE PROPERTIES OF METALS AND NON-METALS

items.label: text
items.text: There are many differences between the properties of metals and non-metals. Here, we will use two main ones to classify them: electrical conductivity and the acid-base character of their oxides.

items.label: text
items.text: Metals conduct electricity and non-metals do not generally conduct electricity. The reason that metals conduct electricity will be explained in Chapter 9 (it is due to the presence of delocalised electrons that are free to move). You may be familiar with the use of metals such as copper in electrical wires.

items.label: text
items.text: Non-metals do not conduct electricity (because there are no electrons that are free to move or mobile ions) but there are a few exceptions, such as graphite (a form of carbon) and silicon.

items.label: text

items.text: The reactions between bases and acids will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 17.

items.label: text
items.text: Non-metals generally form acidic oxides. You may be familiar, for example, with sulfur(IV) oxide (SO2) being one of the gases responsible for acid rain. Acidic oxides react with bases/alkalis to form salts. For example, carbon dioxide, an acidic oxide, reacts with sodium hydroxide, an alkali:
